items.question: When do the more than forty men plan to kill Paul?
items.answer: Before he reaches the priests and elders
items.competitor: When he is before the Sanhedrin

window_text.12: The next morning some Jews formed a conspiracy and bound themselves with an oath not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul.
window_text.13: More than forty men were involved in this plot.
window_text.14: They went to the chief priests and the elders and said, “We have taken a solemn oath not to eat anything until we have killed Paul.
window_text.15: Now then, you and the Sanhedrin petition the commander to bring him before you on the pretext of wanting more accurate information about his case. We are ready to kill him before he gets here.”

items.original_question: When do the more than forty men plan to kill Paul?
items.original_answer: Before he reaches the priests and elders

blind.question: When do the more than forty men plan to kill Paul?

readings.support: We are ready to kill him before he gets here.

assessments.reason: The text says, “We are ready to kill him before he gets here,” with “here” referring to the chief priests and elders/Sanhedrin, matching “before he reaches the priests and elders.”

blind.reason: Verse 15 explicitly states they plan to kill Paul “before he gets here,” i.e., before he reaches the priests and elders.

editor.quote: We are ready to kill him before he gets here.
editor.contrast: Killing Paul before he reaches the priests, elders, and Sanhedrin versus killing him while he is before the Sanhedrin.
editor.reason: The alternative reading is plausible because the conspirators ask for Paul to be brought before the council, but they explicitly say they will kill him before he arrives. The key correctly captures that timing.

reader.quote: We are ready to kill him before he gets here.
reader.contrast: The men intend to ambush Paul before he reaches the priests, elders, and Sanhedrin, not kill him once he is before the Sanhedrin.
reader.reason: The final sentence directly establishes the timing, while “here” refers to the destination to which the commander would bring Paul.

items.question: Who has something to tell the commander?

window_text.16: But when the son of Paul’s sister heard of this plot, he went into the barracks and told Paul.
window_text.17: Then Paul called one of the centurions and said, “Take this young man to the commander; he has something to tell him.”
window_text.18: So he took him to the commander. The centurion said, “Paul, the prisoner, sent for me and asked me to bring this young man to you because he has something to tell you.”

items.original_question: Who has something to tell the commander?

blind.question: Who has something to tell the commander?

readings.support: Take this young man to the commander; he has something to tell him.

assessments.reason: The passage states, “Take this young man to the commander; he has something to tell him,” clearly identifying the young man as the one with something to tell the commander.

blind.reason: The text explicitly identifies “the young man” as the one who has something to tell the commander.

editor.quote: Take this young man to the commander; he has something to tell him.
editor.contrast: The young man has information for the commander; Paul only directs the centurion to bring him.
editor.reason: Paul is a plausible alternative because he summons and instructs the centurion, but both Paul’s words and the centurion’s report identify the young man as the one with something to tell the commander.

reader.quote: “Take this young man to the commander; he has something to tell him.”
reader.contrast: The young man has the information, while Paul only directs the centurion to bring him to the commander.
reader.reason: The quoted instruction identifies the young man as the person with something to tell. Paul arranges the meeting but is not the intended answer.

items.question: Whose consent are the ambushers waiting for now?

window_text.19: The commander took the young man by the hand, drew him aside and asked, “What is it you want to tell me?”
window_text.20: He said: “Some Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul before the Sanhedrin tomorrow on the pretext of wanting more accurate information about him.
window_text.21: Don’t give in to them, because more than forty of them are waiting in ambush for him. They have taken an oath not to eat or drink until they have killed him. They are ready now, waiting for your consent to their request.”
window_text.22: The commander dismissed the young man with this warning: “Don’t tell anyone that you have reported this to me.”

items.original_question: Whose consent are the ambushers waiting for now?

blind.question: Whose consent are the ambushers waiting for now?

readings.support: The commander | waiting for your consent

assessments.reason: In v.21 the young man says they are “waiting for your consent,” and he is speaking to the commander (v.19), so the consent is the commander’s.

blind.reason: Verse 21 explicitly says the ambushers are waiting for “your consent,” referring to the commander addressed in verse 19.

editor.quote: They are ready now, waiting for your consent to their request.
editor.contrast: Whether “your” refers to the commander being addressed or to the Sanhedrin.
editor.reason: The young man is speaking directly to the commander, while the Sanhedrin is mentioned in the third person. Thus “your consent” uniquely means the commander’s consent.

reader.quote: They are ready now, waiting for your consent to their request.
reader.contrast: The commander’s consent versus the Sanhedrin’s consent.
reader.reason: The young man is speaking directly to the commander, so “your consent” refers to the commander’s. Resolving the addressee of “your” is necessary to identify whose approval the ambushers need.

items.question: Who receives the order to ready the force?

window_text.23: Then he called two of his centurions and ordered them, “Get ready a detachment of two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen to go to Caesarea at nine tonight.
window_text.24: Provide horses for Paul so that he may be taken safely to Governor Felix.”

items.original_question: Who receives the order to ready the force?

blind.question: Who receives the order to ready the force?

readings.support: he called two of his centurions and ordered them

assessments.reason: The passage says, “he called two of his centurions and ordered them,” so the recipients of the order are the two centurions.

blind.reason: The verse explicitly states the order was given to the two centurions.

reader.quote: Then he called two of his centurions and ordered them
reader.contrast: the two centurions who receive the order versus the soldiers they are told to ready
reader.reason: “Them” refers to the two centurions whom he called, while the two hundred soldiers are part of the force the centurions must prepare.

editor.quote: he called two of his centurions and ordered them
editor.contrast: The two centurions receive the order; the two hundred soldiers are part of the force they must ready.
editor.reason: The pronoun “them” refers to the two centurions whom he called, clearly identifying the recipients of the order rather than the personnel to be assembled.

items.question: Why did the rescuer bring the man to the Jews' council?
items.answer: to learn why the Jews accuse the man
items.competitor: because of a plot against the man

window_text.27: This man was seized by the Jews and they were about to kill him, but I came with my troops and rescued him, for I had learned that he is a Roman citizen.
window_text.28: I wanted to know why they were accusing him, so I brought him to their Sanhedrin.
window_text.29: I found that the accusation had to do with questions about their law, but there was no charge against him that deserved death or imprisonment.
window_text.30: When I was informed of a plot to be carried out against the man, I sent him to you at once. I also ordered his accusers to present to you their case against him.

items.original_question: Why did the rescuer bring the man to the Jews' council?
items.original_answer: to learn why the Jews accuse the man

blind.question: Why did the rescuer bring the man to the Jews' council?

readings.answer: To find out why they were accusing him.
readings.support: I wanted to know why they were accusing him, so I brought him to their Sanhedrin.

assessments.reason: The passage states, “I wanted to know why they were accusing him, so I brought him to their Sanhedrin,” which matches the key’s purpose of learning why the Jews accused the man.

blind.reason: Verse 28 explicitly explains he brought him to the Sanhedrin to find out the reason for the accusations.

editor.quote: I wanted to know why they were accusing him, so I brought him to their Sanhedrin.
editor.contrast: He brought the man to the Sanhedrin to learn the reason for the accusations, whereas the plot later caused him to send the man to the letter’s recipient.
editor.reason: The stated purpose of bringing him before the council directly matches the key. The competing purpose belongs to a separate, later action.

reader.quote: I wanted to know why they were accusing him, so I brought him to their Sanhedrin.
reader.contrast: He brought the man before the council to investigate the Jews’ accusations, not because of the later plot against him.
reader.reason: Verse 28 directly states the purpose of bringing him to the Sanhedrin. The plot instead explains why he was later sent to the letter’s recipient.
